chief_complaint: finger catching or locking in flexed position, painful nodule
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with finger catching or locking in flexed position, painful nodule. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the tender lump in his palm is a cyst or a fatty tumor that is physically jamming his finger joint.
concerns: He is worried that the nodule in his palm might be a malignant growth or that his finger will freeze permanently bent.
expectations: He hopes to have the lump checked to ensure it is not cancerous and get a steroid shot to stop the locking.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Trigger Finger: Corticosteroid injection, splinting, surgical release if locked, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dupuytren's contracture without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

must_ask.say: Does the finger get stuck bent, and do you need to force it straight?
Can you feel a small lump at the base of that finger?

must_ask.objective: Ask about diabetes or other risk factors

How is this affecting your ability to use your hand?

must_ask.say: We'll try a steroid injection first, and if the finger keeps locking, a small surgical release can fix it.

history.answer: My right ring finger keeps catching and locking when I bend it, and I noticed a painful little lump at the base of the finger.
It is just the base of my right ring finger in the palm; no other fingers or joints on either hand are affected.
It started about three weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse.
It feels like a dull ache in my palm that turns into a sharp pain whenever the finger catches or snaps straight, about four out of ten.
There is no redness or heat, just a small tender bump right where the finger connects to my palm.
It is much stiffer and locked tight when I first wake up in the morning, taking about half an hour to loosen up slightly.
Repetitive gripping or using tools makes the catching worse, while resting and gently massaging the palm gives some relief.
When I bend my finger all the way, it gets stuck in my palm and I usually have to use my other hand to snap it back straight.
Yes, there is a distinct little marble-sized knot right at the crease of my palm that hurts when pressed.
It makes gripping things, typing, and holding utensils difficult because my finger suddenly gets stuck.
No, I have had no fever or chills at all.
I did not injure or twist my hand, but there is a clear popping snap whenever the finger unlocks.
No, I have never had this kind of finger locking or joint trouble before.
I have felt somewhat tired recently from work, but I have not had any fever or lost weight.
No, I have not had any skin rashes, mouth ulcers, hair loss, or redness in my eyes.
No, I do not have morning back stiffness, heel pain, or swelling of my whole fingers or toes.
No, I haven't had diarrhea, painful urination, penile discharge, or any sore throat.
I only have one or two beers on occasion, I don't gorge on meat or seafood, and I don't take water pills.
No, I have never taken steroids or immunosuppressants, and I've never had any joint injections or surgeries.
I have been married and monogamous with my wife for twenty years, with no outside partners.

I felt that hard little lump in my palm, so I thought it might be a cyst or some kind of tumor jamming the joint when I bend it. I'm really worried that this lump might be cancerous, or that my finger will get stuck bent like this permanently.
I hope you can check this lump to make sure it's benign and give me an injection or splint to stop the finger from snapping.
I have no chronic medical conditions like diabetes, high blood pressure, or thyroid disease.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially, maybe one or two beers once a month.
I work as an office manager doing lots of computer work, and I live with my wife.
No one in my family has had rheumatoid arthritis, gout, or hand deformities.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and comfortable middle-aged male in no acute distress, holding the right hand cautiously.

A tender palpable nodule is present over the right fourth metacarpophalangeal joint at the distal palmar crease; active flexion produces a palpable click and mechanical locking in flexion, with no warmth or erythema.
Motor strength is 5/5 in all upper extremity muscle groups bilaterally, with active finger extension mechanically hindered by locking on the right side.
Intact sensation to light touch and pinprick across all digital nerve distributions in both hands.
No palmar fascial thickening or cords, skin puckering, tophi, nail pitting, or rashes noted.
